title: Treatment involving patient's family cuts mental health hospital admissions, study finds
description: Involving a patient's family and friends as part of a new approach to mental health treatment makes it three times less likely they will be admitted t
body: Involving a patient's family and friends as part of a new approach to mental health treatment makes it three times less likely they will be admitted to psychiatric hospital, research has found.Patients rated their recovery and quality of life more highly than those who were treated in the traditional way, the study published in The Lancet Psychiatry, external also found.It is the first major study of Open Dialogue, a way of providing treatment and organising mental health services that involves focusing on the patient's priorities, seeing the same clinicians, and involving people close to them.But, the trial, in five NHS trust areas, found it did not stop patients suffering relapses, and some critics say there needs to be further research into its effectiveness.Dr Nihad Fathi has benefited from the approach after he felt his life started to spiral out of control as the Covid pandemic took hold in 2020.By the next summer, problems in his work had left him feeling anxious, depressed and worthless. He felt like he was letting his clients down."It was so much pressure, stress," he said.He contemplated ending his life."I caught myself like a lost child and I didn't know what's going on in my mind," he said.It was a terrifying time for his wife Farah. "At that stage, I didn't know what to do," she said.For one of his sessions Nihad and Farah sit in a circle in their east London home with two clinicians – consultant psychiatrist Dr Bill Travers and community psychiatric nurse David Adebayo.They have been working with Nihad for five years and the NHS trust they work for, North East London NHS Foundation Trust, has been using Open Dialogue with some of its community patients since 2019.Open Dialogue was first devised in the 1980s in Finland. It is now used in more than 20 countries around the world, although the research into its effectiveness has been limited.The idea is for a patient to regularly take part in "network meetings". As well as two Open Dialogue practitioners, these meetings also involve the friends, families, neighbours or colleagues of the patient. They then remain involved in the patient's recovery.The sessions allow a free-flowing conversation about how the patient feels, what help they would like and how that may be achieved. It also allows the "network" to talk about what they have observed about the patient and their own feelings.Dr Travers said although the network meetings were longer than a normal appointment, the patients need fewer of them."It enables you to reach a much firmer and deeper understanding of the underlying reasons for the problems and indeed to seek solutions that come very much from the person and their family," he said.The study, led by University College London, involved 500 patients that had approached mental health services in crisis. They were split into two groups - one was entered into Open Dialogue, the other received treatment as usual.Researchers found there was no significant difference in whether a patient had a relapse of their illness. But, as well as the reduction in need for psychiatric hospital, if patients in the Open Dialogue group did need to be admitted, the length of time they spent there was on average half that of the other group. There were also improvements in how the patients felt about their wellbeing and recovery.Dr Russell Razzaque, a consultant psychiatrist and the clinical lead on the trial, said this could have significant implications for how the NHS runs psychiatric care."There's a substantial reduction in cost because you're not spending all the money on inpatient beds, which are the most expensive part of the system," he said."So yes, you might be spending a bit more time in the community, but that is what the NHS wants."However, consultant psychiatrist Dr Sameer Jauhar feels the benefits seen in the trial might be explained by the extra resources put into it, and that more research is needed."The important question is whether the distinctive, resource-intensive elements of Open Dialogue itself add benefit beyond good, adequately staffed community care. On the evidence of this trial, that question remains unresolved," he said.But for Farah, Open Dialogue was the right intervention for Nihad."It needs somebody to hear him, somebody to understand him, how he feels, what he's trying to even to achieve. They are helping him and then he sees a better picture," she said.If you are suffering distress or despair, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line

schema.headline: Treatment involving patient's family cuts mental health hospital admissions, study finds

title: Aunt who died in Middlesbrough house fire was 'beautiful soul'
description: A woman killed in a house fire has been described by her mother as "a beautiful soul, who would have done anything for anybody".Natalie McDonald, 34,
body: A woman killed in a house fire has been described by her mother as "a beautiful soul, who would have done anything for anybody".Natalie McDonald, 34, died along with her seven-year-old niece, Valentina Foster, in the blaze in Grangetown, near Middlesbrough, in the early hours of Wednesday.Cleveland Police said the fire had also left a 48-year-old woman in a critical condition in hospital alongside another three people who suffered non-life threatening injuries.Two men, aged 23 and 31, had been arrested on suspicion of murder and were in police custody, the force said.Lisa Kirton, Natalie's mother, told the BBC her daughter was "lovely, bright and bubbly" and "everybody loved her".She said Valentina, also known as Tina, had been spending the summer holidays with the family."She was a cute little kid," Kirton said. "I can't believe it, seven years old - it's just a disgrace."She also said Natalie's 15-year-old daughter and a friend had managed to escape through an upstairs window. The friend, she said, had "kicked out a window" and "had saved their lives".On Wednesday, Police officers guarded a cordon around the scene and Northern Powergrid staff were also on site.Cleveland Fire Brigade said it had sent six fire engines and the Incident Command Unit.At 13:30 BST it confirmed the fire had been extinguished, but one engine remained on "proactive standby".A spokesperson said road closures were in place and asked members of the public to avoid the area where possible.They also said the "tragic incident" was being jointly investigated by the fire service and Cleveland Police.Cleveland Police said it was "keeping an open mind and cannot rule out any links to wider organised crime at this time".The fire happened about two miles from the A66 crash that killed five young men and two police officers on Saturday morning.Redcar and Cleveland Local Policing Commander Supt Emily Harrison said the force was working to "establish the circumstances of exactly what has happened"."We will have a high visibility presence in the Grangetown area and encourage anyone who has concerns, or who may have information, to approach our officers."Patrols had been increased in the local area to "reassure the local community", the force said earlier.Grangetown councillor Adam Brook urged people not to speculate or share unconfirmed information.Redcar MP Anna Turley said the community had faced a "profound amount of heartbreak over the past few weeks" and expressed her condolences to the loved ones of those who died and were injured.The families of the people involved have been informed and are being supported by specialist officers.Follow BBC Tees on X,, external Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external and listen to Radio Tees on BBC Sounds.

schema.headline: Aunt who died in Middlesbrough house fire was 'beautiful soul'

title: First patient to have brain surgery with real-time AI assistance
description: The world's first patient to have brain surgery with live artificial intelligence assistance has successfully had his tumour removed.Rhys Hibbert, a f
body: The world's first patient to have brain surgery with live artificial intelligence assistance has successfully had his tumour removed.Rhys Hibbert, a father-of-two from Bedfordshire, could have lost his sight without the operation, said surgeons at University College London Hospital.The AI tool analysed a video feed of the operation as it happened and advised surgeons on how to avoid crucial but hidden vessels and nerves in the brain. It allowed them to safely remove as much of the tumour as possible."From a patient safety perspective, I can see absolutely the benefit. There are no road signs inside our head," said Hibbert. Until 18 months ago, 48-year-old Hibbert, a customer services manager, was fit and healthy, going on a two-mile walk every lunchtime.It was on one of these walks that he fell unconscious and started fitting in the road.A brain scan revealed he had an 11mm (0.433in) non-cancerous tumour growing on the pituitary gland - a marble-sized organ at the base of the skull. The gland secretes vital hormones that help with processes like growth, metabolism and regulating blood pressure and temperature.Crucially it sits very close to the carotid arteries which are vital vessels that supply blood to the brain, and the optic nerves that control vision. As Hibbert's tumour began to press on his optic nerves, it narrowed his peripheral vision. Although he didn't need surgery straight away Hibbert started to trip over things and felt severely fatigued and dizzy."For 18 years of married life I've always got out of bed and made my wife a cup of coffee," Hibbert said, "and I wasn't going to let this tumour stop that."  He said the biggest impacts for him were emotional and psychological."Though I had a lot of people kindly offering help, you don't want to be a burden on people," he added.When surgeons gave him the option to be the first person to try the operation with their bespoke AI tool involved, he didn't hesitate."If patients are not prepared to join research how can doctors ever learn and how can medicine ever progress?" he said.The surgery involved inserting an endoscope - a thin camera on a stick - via the nose to the base of the skull. At this point the tumour was close but hidden behind layers of  bone and tough membrane.Identifying the safest place to extract it was not straightforward, particularly as anatomy tends to differ between individuals. Complication rates vary but there was a 25–50% chance of not getting the whole tumour out and a 0.5–2% chance of injuring a major blood vessel. This is where the AI tool came in. On a second screen it analysed the live video feed,, tracked the surgical instruments, and marked up areas where the vessels and nerves were most likely to be, highlighting areas where it is safest to remove the tumour.It is similar to facial recognition technology on phones, but recognises important and often hidden anatomical structures instead.The average UK surgeon performs about 10 to 20 of these operations a year, relying on scans done before surgery to familiarise themselves with the patient's anatomy.Researchers trained and evaluated their AI system on hundreds of videos of pituitary tumour removals - carefully drawing around the vessels and nerves on each video to help the system capture data and begin to "recognise" the most important structures. "It is trained on more operations than most surgeons see or do in a lifetime and can act like an expert second pair of eyes," said Prof Hani Marcus, who helped carry out the procedure. And unlike other experimental AI tools, it works in real time, he added.

schema.headline: First patient to have brain surgery with real-time AI assistance

title: England v Pakistan: Joe Root shows himself to be the leader England need
description: At the back of the Compton Stand at Lord's is an enormous picture of Ben Stokes.In the snap, Stokes unleashes a bouncer to a flinching Mohammed Siraj,
body: At the back of the Compton Stand at Lord's is an enormous picture of Ben Stokes.In the snap, Stokes unleashes a bouncer to a flinching Mohammed Siraj, the India tailender. It was taken during England's heart-stopping 22-run win on this ground last summer.England's defeat of India was all about Stokes. He made contributions with the bat in both innings, ran out Rishabh Pant with a direct hit and put in a trademark marathon bowling spell on the final day. Stokes came to the post-match media conference with blood seeping through his sock.Throughout Stokes' tenure as England captain, the question loomed of how anyone would eventually go about succeeding him.For better or worse, Stokes became the all-encompassing figure in the team, for his performances on the field and what he said or did off it. It was hard to imagine how anyone could emerge from his shadow without having their leadership compared to the talismanic all-rounder.England are little more than a week into the post-Stokes era and there is already no doubt about the strength of leadership at the helm. This is Joe Root's team now.The last thing Root would have wanted at the beginning of his second reign as skipper was the Brydon Carse controversy.Yet, the Yorkshireman has shown himself to be the captain English cricket needs, yet probably does not deserve.Root's measured, assured and honest address to the media at Lord's on Tuesday was the most impressive display of leadership from anyone connected with the England team in a long time.Perhaps Root is helped by the circumstances. If Brendon McCullum was still around, he would have been pushed in front of cameras, but McCullum has gone and his replacement Stephen Fleming is yet to arrive. It leaves Root as unquestionably the man in charge.In terms of Root's second coming as skipper, the off-field part might be the easy bit. It is on the field where he now has a point to prove.He said as much last week before the Headingley Test - that the biggest challenge in resuming the captaincy was overcoming the perceptions others have of his leadership.It is not that Root was an awful captain first time around - far from it. It is just the abiding memory is an awful ending of only one win from 17 matches, a horror run that left Root and his team broken.Leeds was a dream restart, an innings win over Pakistan wrapped up inside three days.But the one-sided nature of that victory did not give Root room to show what kind of on-field captain he will be this time around. His best act at Headingley was to win the toss and, after Ollie Robinson took a wicket with the first ball of the match, England were on top.There have been glimpses of what the New Root could become.Stokes' preference for naming an England team two days before a Test has gone, at least for now. England are likely to be unchanged at Lord's, though that will not be confirmed until the toss.Root has removed himself from first slip and now fields at mid-off. It may only be a temporary move, but it puts him closer to his bowlers. On the first morning at Headingley, Root yanked a wayward Jofra Archer from the attack after only two overs. It is hard to imagine he would have done the same to either Stuart Broad or James Anderson.There was a hint of funkiness in the field, albeit an overhang from Root's first spell as captain. The dismissal of Azan Awais in Pakistan's second innings was the eighth time a seamer under Root has had a catch taken at leg slip - the most of any captain since such data began being collected in 2006.Asked what the difference was between the captaincy of Stokes and Root, fast bowler Josh Tongue said: "It's very chilled out there." Tongue probably did not mean to imply Root brings a greater calmness than Stokes, yet few would argue he has taken the intensity down a notch or two.For all the impressive media conferences, bowling changes and leg slips, Root will be judged on results, and a win this week would give England their first series triumph since 2024.There will be plenty of attention on the Lord's pitch, so heavily criticised after England's win against New Zealand. On Wednesday, Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC) chairman Mark Nicholas and director of cricket Rob Lynch were seen taking a good look at the surface.Pakistan should be better than their showing at Headingley, mainly because they cannot get much worse. They are boosted by the return of captain Babar Azam from a hand injury and have won the previous two Tests they have played here.England will want to build on the green shoots of recovery that sprouted in Leeds.Jordan Cox impressed at number three and is highly rated by the management. There could be a logjam in the top order when Jacob Bethell returns to fitness, so all of Cox, Emilio Gay, Dan Lawrence and Jamie Smith will want to ensure they are not squeezed out.Root said his quartet of fast bowlers "do not know how good they can be". That foursome now have the opportunity to show they can be England's first-choice attack in a range of conditions. It is a bad time for Carse to put himself out of the picture.As for Root, no man has more runs or hundreds on this ground. Now he returns as the captain, already leading by example this week."When you have the privilege of being a leader within a team, you want to build something bigger than just winning," he said. "I feel like I didn't do that very well first time around."There's a lot to look forward to, there's a lot to work hard towards. I guess that's the fun side of it."For Root and his players, following the past few days, the fun side will simply be returning to playing cricket.

schema.headline: England v Pakistan: Joe Root shows himself to be the leader England need

title: How Dolly Parton's business acumen helped her succeed far beyond the charts
description: Not many musicians would snub a chance to work with Elvis Presley. But when Dolly Parton did so, it made her millions.In 1974, after writing and recor
body: Not many musicians would snub a chance to work with Elvis Presley. But when Dolly Parton did so, it made her millions.In 1974, after writing and recording I Will Always Love You, Parton was asked if Presley could cover the song. She turned him down after his manager demanded half the rights."Of course, I cried all night about that," she later said of the ordeal in an interview.But she wasn't crying in 1992 when Whitney Houston's power-ballad cover became a hit. Global sales of the song topped 20 million, earning Parton more than $10m in royalties, according to business magazine Forbes.This is the less well-known side of Parton. While country music and films brought her fame, her entrepreneurial zeal brought her fortune.The country icon signed deals, started companies, and invested in ideas that Forbes says built her a net worth of $450m by the time she died.Parton wasn't always wealthy. She grew up in poverty and in her 1971 hit Coat of Many Colours describes how she would wear rags to school which her "mama" had knitted together.In a 2017 BBC interview, she said her father gave her business lessons from early in her career."My dad wasn't an educated man, he wasn't able to read and write, but my daddy had a great sense of business," she told the BBC's World Service in 2017."So when I got into the music business, I thought of it as a business. And so I started early on keeping my own songs and my own publishing company."While her publishing company helped build her wealth, Parton had plenty of other business ideas.In 1985, she co-founded a film and TV production company called Sandollar Productions, which helped to make 90s cult thriller Buffy The Vampire Slayer. Then there was Dollywood - the theme park in in the foothills of the Smoky Mountains in her home state of Tennessee, which she became co-owner of in 1986. It had changed owners multiple times since it was first set up 25 years earlier and her buy-in exponentially boosted visitor numbers. She kept improving the park. In 2015, she opened the DreamMore Resort, a four-star hotel and spa down the road from Dollywood. Today, many of Parton's family members work at the theme park and it is the biggest employer in its county. She launched the Dolly Beauty cosmetics line in 2025 and she opened Dolly's Tennessean Travel Stop in June this year. The shop offers a signature coffee brand named Cup of Ambition, a nod to her Grammy-winning single 9 to 5.Paul Milliken, a reporter from Fox 5 Atlanta who had interviewed Parton many times, said diversification was the key to her business success."It's a lesson that continues from her to this day to young artists," he told BBC's Wake Up to Money.Parton may have been motivated to make money right into her 80s, but she told the BBC in the 2017 interview that she never lost sight of where she came from."Being brought up poor means I don't take things for granted, and no matter how much money I make, I'll always count my blessings quicker and more often than I count my money.She has "always realised the value of a dollar", too."Even now if I go in a store it's hard for me to pay a huge amount of money for one item. I say 'good Lord', what could mummy and daddy have done with that!"Wealth was more than just a means to an end for Parton. It also allowed her to be generous.She gave millions away to funding child literacy, providing wildfire relief, and creating a cure for Covid-19. In 2022, she was awarded the Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy for her charity work.Talking about her many business and charity ideas in 2017, she told the BBC: "I just wish I was 30 years old so I could start over again and get all this stuff done... I'm gonna' be working till I fall over bad."

schema.headline: How Dolly Parton's business acumen helped her succeed far beyond the charts

title: Yayoi Kusama: Japanese avant-garde artist dies aged 97
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Polka-dots, pumpkins and infinity room mirrors are hallmarks of Kusama's artistryByKurumi MoriTokyo correspondent
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Polka-dots, pumpkins and infinity room mirrors are hallmarks of Kusama's artistryByKurumi MoriTokyo correspondent and Harry SekulichUpdated 40 minutes agoJapanese avant-garde artist Yayoi Kusama, who became famous for her colourful polka dot-covered sculptures and installations, has died at the age of 97.Kusama, who had voluntarily lived in a psychiatric hospital for decades, was known for her bright red wig and her giant, quirky creations.Her exhibitions drew large crowds to galleries around the world, and her vibrant works fetched some of the highest ever prices for a female artist.A statement from her company said: "Throughout an extraordinary lifetime devoted entirely to artistic creation, Kusama pursued an internationally acclaimed career as a pioneering avant-garde artist whose creative practice encompassed visual art, performance, fiction, and poetry."Image source, Getty ImagesKusama died at a hospital in Tokyo on 14 August, the statement said.It added: "She continued to paint until her final days, never setting aside her brush, and continued exploration of forever love and eternal soul."We will carry forward Kusama's wishes and, through art, continue to bring hope and strength for the future to people around the world."Kusama became one of the world's most recognisable artists and a global cultural icon in her 80s and 90s, after having been mostly overlooked for decades.Poorly received by a masculine-dominated art scene of New York in the 1960s, Kusama caused a stir with her exhibitions of phallic sculptures, including a fabric couch, and frequent displays of nudity.Image source, NY Daily News via Getty ImagesImage caption, Frequent nudity in her works drew scorn in Kusama's native Japan.In 1965, her work "Infinity Mirror Rooms", in which mirrors and lights create seemingly endless spaces, attracted millions of visitors. Later, her polka-dot and pumpkin works became highly sought-after.However, she became distressed when her ideas were copied by or "inspired" her male contemporaries – including Andy Warhol, Claes Oldenburg and Lucas Samaras – whose works would be displayed at more prestigious galleries.After spending years watching male artists gain recognition for her work, she returned home to Japan – feeling dejected and distraught.She entered a psychiatric facility receiving treatment for mental illnesses, where she would live and work for the remainder of her life.Miraculously, she managed to find a hospital where the doctors were interested in art therapy and checked herself in. Such a secure environment allowed her to focus on creating art.Through the 1970s and early 80s, her work depicted uncharacteristically dark series' of collages in which she embraced the imagery of natural life cycles.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Kusama's Infinity Rooms immersed visitors in the installation using mirrors and lightsKusama went on to become Japan's first solo artist to represent the country at the 1993 Venice Biennale. Twenty-seven years earlier, she had turned up, uninvited, and laid down 1,500 mirror balls on the ground.The roaring success of the exhibition led to a huge transformation in how she was received both in Japan and abroad.In 2001, she was awarded the Asahi Prize – recognising outstanding cultural, academic and artistic contributions in Japan.One of her paintings fetched about $10.5m (£7.7m) at auction in 2022, making her works some of the highest-earning in the world for a female artist.Then, her work appeared in major museums and collaborations with luxury brands including Louis Vuitton.Image source, Chesnot/Getty ImagesImage caption, Sculpture of Yayoi Kusama erected outside Maison Louis Vuitton in Paris, 2023As a child, Kusama experienced hallucinations of embers and flashing – later using her art as a vehicle for others to understand her vision of the world."One day, after seeing a tablecloth with a red flower pattern on a desk, I saw the same red flower pattern all over the ceiling, windows and pillars. It filled the room, and covered my body," she wrote in her autobiography.Kusama was born in 1929 in the rural provincial town of Matsumoto, based in the central Nagano region of Japan.Her parents did not support her early moves to study painting in Kyoto. She was later told that her artistry caused great shame to her conservative family. Some elements of the US press also criticised what they perceived as an endless desire for publicity – either in her messaging promoting peace or critiquing the art establishment.Image caption, Kusama staged a major exhibition in Manchester in 2023The world, along with her native Japan, radically changed its perception of Kusama in her later life.Social media fuelled a spike in interest over recent years – with her museum's bold floral shapes and shiny steel orbs turning into a desired backdrop for selfies and poses.Among her many motifs, the pumpkin has become iconic in her works. To her, the vegetable represented comfort and nostalgia.She once said in an interview, "Pumpkins speak to me.""They embody a sense of stability and gives me peace of mind."In her hometown of Naoshima, visitors coming by ferry are greeted by her outdoor Red Pumpkin sculpture covered in bold, black polka dots.

schema.headline: Yayoi Kusama: Japanese avant-garde artist dies aged 97

title: Is Bukayo Saka getting back to his best at Arsenal?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Bukayo Saka scored 11 goals and provided nine assists in all competitions for Arsenal last seasonByArsenal re
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Bukayo Saka scored 11 goals and provided nine assists in all competitions for Arsenal last seasonByArsenal reporterBukayo Saka's performance in Arsenal's impressive opening-day win has already convinced some fans the Gunners are going to defend their Premier League crown.The 24-year-old's game-time for the north London outfit was managed at the end of last season, as well as with England at the World Cup, because of an Achilles injury he picked up in March.Saka missed the March international break and seven games for the Gunners, but returned to help them lift the Premier League title for the first time in 22 years.The winger was then taken off during the Champions League final as Arsenal lost to Paris-St Germain in Budapest and his performance was criticised. England boss Thomas Tuchel also limited his minutes during the World Cup, but asked if he found it frustrating being judged while not 100% fit, Saka said it was a "gamble" he was willing to take.A rest after the tournament seems to have allowed Saka to start this campaign at his best. He looked sharp against newly promoted Coventry on Friday, giving full-back Jay Dasilva a torrid time while scoring the second goal in the 3-0 win.The sight of Saka flying down the right wing and involved in a lot of Arsenal's attacks will be welcomed by supporters.Because, despite a stop-start season last year, Saka still clocked up 49 appearances for the Gunners and their win percentage was notably more impressive with him in the team.Did Saka's World Cup play a part in this season's sharpness?Saka only started three of England's eight games at the World Cup, including scoring a hat-trick in the 6-4 third-place final win over France.That result secured England's best finish in a World Cup on foreign soil.Saka, though, had been left out of the semi-final defeat by Argentina, despite starting the last-16 win over Mexico and the quarter-final win over Norway.The winger said after the victory against Mexico he wished he had been at 100% fitness going into the tournament but accepted "that hasn't been the case".Saka played just 357 minutes at the World Cup, just 48% of England's total minutes across eight matches at the tournament.He showed flashes of his quality, providing three assists, which alongside Anthony Gordon was the most of any England player, as well as three goals.In fact, he registered a goal involvement on average every 60 minutes for the Three Lions during the tournament.Figure caption, Arsenal start title defence with comfortable win over CoventrySaka's pre-season and signs of top form Saka returned from the World Cup and after a break rejoined the Arsenal squad, playing his first minutes of this season in the Community Shield, coming on when the Gunners were already leading Manchester City 3-0. His acceleration and sharpness during that cameo was something that was lacking towards the end of last season as the winger looked to help his team get over the line. And after his starring performance against Coventry in the first Premier League game of the season, he hinted that after low minutes at the World Cup and a summer break he felt back to his best."I was training a lot so I could be ready for the start of the season and ready to help the team in the way I know I can," Saka said in the mixed zone after the win."It was more about balancing my time off and not having too much of a break. I took seven days off and then started to train again."I've put in a lot of work since then and I'm feeling good. I just tried to come back in good shape, so I'm on top of my body."That motivation seems to have come from the frustration of not achieving England's goal at the World Cup, with the winger returning to training a few days early."The World Cup didn't necessarily go how I wanted it to, for myself and for the team as well," he said."I felt really hungry after the World Cup, after the season ended. I was looking forward to this new season." Havertz, Saka, Odegaard and White partnershipAnother part of why Saka looks like he is in a flow state so early in the season is the return of Kai Havertz, Martin Odegaard and Ben White to full fitness.There is no debate that White and Saka's partnership down the right-hand side, with the defender's overlapping runs, unlock the best in Saka.The partnership he has with Odegaard and Havertz is also crucial to a fluid Arsenal attack and the win over Coventry was just the second time since December 2024 that the trio started a Premier League game together, such have been their injury problems.There have been questions about whether Arteta is too reliant on Saka, and before the start of this season the winger had played 153 matches, with 61 of them being the full 90 minutes, across the past three seasons.But with an enforced break through injury and then lower minutes at the World Cup, he could be about to produce the regular scintillating performances we have become used to.

schema.headline: Is Bukayo Saka getting back to his best at Arsenal?

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Britons lost in Nepal flood' and 'Regal has landed'
description: The front page of the Times, external charts the destruction at the Nepal-Tibet border with images of people running for their lives as mud, water and
body: The front page of the Times, external charts the destruction at the Nepal-Tibet border with images of people running for their lives as mud, water and debris engulf a building. The Daily Mail describes, external the disaster as an  "apocalyptic mudslide" that "wiped out everything in its path".  The paper says witnesses thought they were seeing explosions caused by a military invasion, as clouds of debris were thrown up into the air.The i Paper, external on Meta's decision to pay billions of dollars to settle claims - which it denies - that Facebook and Instagram harmed children. The paper notes the firm's agreement to make apps safer for young people will not apply to the UK.The Guardian's analysis, external calls the introduction of default protections for teens "a major concession", that "sets a precedent others in the tech industry are likely to follow".  "Well that's told 'em", quips the Sun's columnist, external, Colin Robertson, who points out the cost of the settlement represents just over one per cent of Meta's $1.4 trillion value.The Daily Telegraph says, external it understands that Germany is in talks to invest in Britain's nuclear deterrent, as part of efforts to reduce Europe's reliance on the US.  The paper says military planners in Berlin believe they could contribute air defences to key locations, such as the base in Faslane that houses submarines armed with the UK's Trident missiles.Andy Burnham has spoken the Financial Times, external in what it describes as his "most pro-business interview since becoming prime minister". He tells the FT he's "acutely conscious of how hard the operating environment is for businesses", but declines to say whether taxes on companies would rise in the upcoming Budget.The coverage of the outpouring of affection for the late queen of country, Dolly Parton, spills into a second day, with jourrnalists who were lucky enough to interview her setting out their memories.  In the Daily Express, external, Paul Sexton describes her as "side-splittingly funny" and "bigger than country music itself". The Daily Mirror's, external Tom Bryant recalls how she made him feel "at the centre of her world, despite her enormous fame".

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'Britons lost in Nepal flood' and 'Regal has landed'

title: Six essential skills employers say job seekers should have to stand out
description: One of the big shocks for many leaving education and trying to get into work is the sudden lack of structure, so being able to prioritise your own wor
body: One of the big shocks for many leaving education and trying to get into work is the sudden lack of structure, so being able to prioritise your own work is seen by many employers as essential.In Leeds, Christian Townsley, the co-founder of the North Bar group, says working in a busy bar is all about staying calm and keeping a "cool head"."It's important that you can organise, you can multitask, you can identify who's next at the bar and remember that," he says.Townsley offers trial shifts as part of the recruitment process, to give job seekers an opportunity to showcase these skills in action."We'll observe them working with customers, working with the team, seeing how they fit in, seeing how they communicate," he says.As people get promoted, they are expected to take on more responsibilities and be able to manage them within the role."There's organisation, ordering beer, pricing beer, planning social media, marketing, recruiting," Townsley adds.Jude Hillary, the economist who led the project for NFER, says these human skills are what will allow people to get into and keep work at a higher skill level, even while automation bites."This is where the job growth is going to be in the labour market," he says. "It's really important young people come into the labour market being able to compete for these jobs."And he believes focusing on these six essential employment skills will help young people adapt in a time of huge change."It's increasingly likely that during the course of your working life, you might have to make some fairly dramatic changes in what you're doing as your job gets replaced by technology."An independent review led by Alan Milburn, a former health secretary, has been looking at the scale of young people not working, learning or training.The interim report said 42% of employers listed a lack of soft skills or work readiness as a challenge when hiring young people. Only 10% cited the resilience of young people which was the next biggest concern.There is increasing pressure for schools, colleges and universities to focus on giving young people what they need to be work-ready alongside academic learning.Already, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has signalled that more teenagers should start technical education at 14 and has supported a work experience scheme for 10,000 young people announced this week by the retail chain Sainsbury's.In September, the final report of the Milburn review is expected to set out its proposals on how to get more young adults into secure work.Additional reporting by Hannah Karpel.

schema.headline: Six essential skills employers say job seekers should have to stand out

title: What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods
description: Figure caption, Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet borderByOlivia IrelandUpdated 2 hours agoMassive landslides and flash floods on t
body: Figure caption, Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet borderByOlivia IrelandUpdated 2 hours agoMassive landslides and flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have caused widespread damage and left hundreds dead or missing.Search and rescue operations are under way. Chinese state media has said there are significant casualties, while Nepalese officials anticipate "huge scale loss".Here is what we know so far.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Buildings were submerged in Nepal's Nuwakot districtWhat caused the deadly landslide?Nepal's foreign minister earlier said an earthquake was reported on the Tibet-Nepal border shortly before the landslide, suggesting it may have triggered the disaster.But the United States Geological Survey's latest analysis suggests there was no earthquake, raising questions about what caused the landslide itself.One possibility is that water from rainfall or melting ice may have destabilised the ground or ice, triggering a chain reaction.Climate change is known to be driving faster glacier melt in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region, but scientists say it is too soon to pinpoint its role in this specific event.Scientists are now trying to piece together the order of events.They'll be looking at satellite images of exactly where the landslide occurred, whether any glacial lakes suddenly drained, and where the river might have become blocked, as well as data on recent rainfall.Figure caption, Watch: BBC Nepali's Shreejana Shrestha is at a hospital in Kathmandu, where some survivors are being flown in by helicopterA deluge of material careered towards northern Nepalese towns, including areas popular with mountaineering tourists and pilgrims. The border is around 40 miles (64.4km) north of Nepal's capital city Kathmandu. Footage showed a wall of mud and rock sweeping away buildings, roads and vehicles, as people fled the fast-moving wave of material in the Nuwakot region.In one video, a towering wall of water and mud was seen rushing down a gorge along the Trishuli River and enveloping the Rasuvagadhi Border check point, a multi-storey building.Severe flooding has been reported along the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers.Deaths have also been reported in villages on the Tibetan side of the border.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Satellite images of Khadga Bhanjyang on the Trishuli River three days apart show the scale of floodingHow many people are dead and missing?The number of people killed or missing is still becoming clear. Nepali police say at least 162 people have died. Among those killed, 64 were found in downstream areas in the Chitwan district while another 26 were found in Nawalparasi East. The number of people missing in the mudslide disaster in Tibet's Gyirong county has risen to 558, China's state broadcaster CCTV said on Thursday.Among these are 260 foreign nationals, CCTV said, adding that the death toll remained at three.The border at Gyirong is the main crossing point for tourists and traffic between China and Nepal.Nepal had earlier also said that some 579 tourists were missing, with 466 foreigners among them. It is not clear if any of the missing in the Nepali and Chinese figures have been counted twice.Image source, ReutersHow are governments responding?Nepal's prime minister said "the entire nation has been left shocked and deeply distressed" and that officials would coordinate with China on the response. China's President Xi Jinping urged an "all-out" search effort, and promised stronger monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary impacts.In neighbouring India, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said his government was "prepared to provide Nepal with all possible types of humanitarian assistance". UN Secretary General António Guterres says he is "saddened by the severe flooding", adding that UN teams and partners are mobilising supplies and personnel in Nepal to support the government-led response.The US has promised $500,000 in aid which will be used to cover emergency shelter, water, sanitation and other relief items for communities affected by the floods.UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the British government would do "everything we can" to support British nationals in Nepal.Figure caption, Aerial footage shows flash flood on Nepal-Tibet borderWhat countries are the missing tourists from?Tourists from all over the world come to Nepal for its mountains and sacred sites. Official figures suggested at least 291 foreigners are among the missing, including: India - the Nepal Tourism board said 142 nationals from neighbouring India were missingUkraine - Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said Nepal's Tourist Police informed them 53 Ukrainian nationals were missingMalaysia - 17 Malaysians travelling with Fishtail Tours and Travels are missing in the floods, the board said. An official at the Malaysian embassy in Nepal said more than 50 Malaysians were currently unreachableUK - Nepal police have confirmed that 33 British nationals are missingCanada - a tourism board spokesman in Nepal said that 24 Canadians have been reported missingUS - the latest update from Nepal's tourist board is that 54 US tourists are known to be among the missingAustralia - Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has confirmed at least 34 Australian citizens are among the missingSmaller numbers of travellers from South Korea, South Africa, Portugal and the Netherlands are also among the missing.

schema.headline: What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods

title: Iceland holds knife-edge referendum on EU - and it could be decided on fish
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir (C) supports Iceland joining the EUByAdrienne Murrayin Reykjavik
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir (C) supports Iceland joining the EUByAdrienne Murrayin Reykjavik, IcelandInside a waterfront factory, workers in hairnets and blue overalls are sorting freshly caught cod and haddock, and machines process the fish into fillets, mostly bound for Europe.Visir fishing boss Pétur Pálsson, who fears joining the European Union would cost Iceland jobs and drive factories abroad, says: "If we are in the EU, they will be the ones who make the policy."On Saturday, voters in this island nation of almost 400,000 people will decide whether their country should resume talks on joining the EU. It is a referendum that polls suggest is too close to call.Supporters think closer European ties could help tame Iceland's volatile currency and soaring cost of living.Opponents say Iceland's sovereignty and control over "priceless" fishing waters are at stake, and would rather continue going it alone.Image caption, Fisheries and other marine industries make up almost 40% of Iceland's exportsIt is a fault line that has divided Icelanders for decades, but after winning a snap election in 2024 Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir's centre-left government pledged to hold a referendum by 2027.Russia's war in Ukraine, sharpening Arctic rivalries and US President Donald Trump's tariff threats and designs on Greenland have accelerated that timetable."Things have been moving very rapidly with respect to geopolitical challenges," Finance Minister Daði Már Kristófersson tells the BBC, pushing Iceland's place in the world "up the agenda".Iceland lies high in the North Atlantic, adjacent to a strategic stretch of sea called the GIUK gap, where Russian maritime activity is closely watched by the West.It is a founding member of Nato, and yet has no military of its own.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The No-campaign has used the slogan "Iceland for sale? No thanks"One poll this week put the Yes vote ahead by 51.3% to 48.7%; an earlier poll had the two camps neck and neck."It's impossibly [hard] to predict," says Eirikur Bergmann, professor of politics at Bifröst University. "Both camps are throwing everything they have at it."Kristoffersen's Liberal Reform party is a leading voice behind the Yes campaign.He argues that EU membership would strengthen Iceland's security and trade position, and shield it from much bigger powers.There's the economic case too. "We see the opportunity of joining the EU and adopting the euro as a very significant benefit to Icelandic companies and to the Icelandic general public," he says.A Yes vote would kickstart negotiations with Brussels, but a second referendum would have to greenlight any final membership deal. The EU's 27 members would have to agree to it too.A No vote would shelve talks for the time being.Some Icelanders are expected to vote Yes as this is not the final referendum anyway. "We have to know what's in the package from the EU," says Reykjavik resident Anna Ragnarsdottir. "If we say no, we won't ever know."Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Iceland is one of the world's most expensive countries - so economic concerns are a key issue in the EU debateAlthough outside the EU, Iceland is part of the European Economic Area (EEA) along with Norway and Liechtenstein, so it is part of the single market and the Schengen border-free zone.Reykjavik opened EU accession talks two years after the devastating 2008 global financial crisis, but abandoned them in 2013.Fishing was the biggest obstacle then, and remains a dealbreaker today.Fish and marine industries account for almost 40% of Iceland's exports and many No voters are worried that under the EU's common fisheries policy they could cede some control of their lucrative fishing grounds.Opposition leader Guðrún Hafsteinsdóttir, who leads the No campaign, vows Iceland's waters will never be shared.Fishing is inseparable from Iceland's culture and political identity, and no politician ever could make that concession, says Prof Bergmann. "They'd be expelled from the country."Iceland's government intends to carve out a "special arrangement" to protect fishing and agriculture, and the finance minister says they are confident of getting "some exemptions".Non-EU member Norway succeeded in 1994 even though it did not complete the process, he says, while EU states Finland and Sweden secured special terms for agriculture in the far north.But Eurosceptics doubt a carve-out is possible.The head of the Icelandic Farmers' Association, Margrét Ágústa Sigurðardóttir, is unconvinced: "No member state has been granted a permanent opt-out."She fears EU policies will focus on "the interests of 450 million consumers, rather than the specific needs of a country of 400,000 people".Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Iceland has no military, but it is a Nato member and hosts alliance aircraft at Keflavik airportWhen the BBC visited the airbase at Keflavik this month, fighter jets were taking off, and the Stars and Stripes was flapping alongside the Belgian tricolour and Nato flags.With no military, Iceland's security relies on its Nato allies and a 1951 defence pact with the US.However, Trump's repeated comments on taking over Greenland, and the risk of a weakened Nato alliance have added to Iceland's concerns.Officials point to Russia's maritime activities in waters close to Iceland as the main security issue and in June Icelandic authorities said a Russian intelligence ship was tracked passing through Iceland's Exclusive Economic Zone.There was disbelief among Icelanders when Trump mistakenly referred to their country four times in his speech at Davos, when he meant Greenland. The new US ambassador had to apologise when he joked that Iceland could become the 52nd US state.The "special relationship" is unchanged, emphasises Daði Már Kristófersson. Yet, the finance minister believes "an additional pillar is important", and the government signed a defence partnership with the EU in March.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Despite Greenlanders overwhelmingly opposing it, Trump has not dropped his wish to take over the island - something which is weighing on Icelandic votersYet geopolitics, perhaps surprisingly, has been largely absent from Iceland's public debate.For Snærós Sindradóttir of the European Movement in Iceland that is frustrating.The referendum is happening now "100% [because of] security matters", she says.Giant red letters spelling "JA!", meaning yes, fill the windows at the group's campaign office.The Yes camp says EU membership offers greater financial stability, while adopting the euro could curb the country's stubbornly high inflation.Since breaking away from Denmark in 1944, Iceland has transformed from a poor island into one of Europe's most affluent nations.But prices in Iceland were 84% higher than the EU average, according to analysis by the academic union Viska, and interest rates have climbed to 8%."We get higher salaries, and it goes straight to the cost of everything," Sindradottir complains. "It's like a dog chasing its own tail constantly."Image caption, Snærós Sindradóttir is frustrated that the debate ahead of the referendum has not focused on geopoliticsIn downtown Reykjavik it is the high cost of living and sovereignty that people care about most."The biggest problem right now is for the generation who are trying to buy their own housing," says Adolf Fridriksson, 62. "The mortgage rates are terrifying."Meanwhile, Helga, 22, believes joining the EU will be too costly: "The fishing industry, and everything else, should be in our control."Saturday's result is being watched closely across Europe.If the Yes vote wins, Icelandic officials say talks with Brussels will take "months, not years", as 11 of the 35 areas of negotiation were already finalised when they were broken off.Leaders are taking note in neighbouring Norway, a traditionally Eurosceptic country and a fellow member of the EEA. But support for joining the EU is growing there too.Gaining a rich and stable new member in Iceland would be a welcome win for EU enlargement, says Hallgrímur Oddsson, head of the EU-Iceland think-tank European Currents."But a No vote could also be perceived as a loss."

schema.headline: Iceland holds knife-edge referendum on EU - and it could be decided on fish

title: Girl, 13, among 33 UK nationals missing after Nepal flash floods
description: Thirty-three people from the UK are among hundreds feared missing following a deadly flash flood near the Nepal-Tibet border.Flooding and mud slides h
body: Thirty-three people from the UK are among hundreds feared missing following a deadly flash flood near the Nepal-Tibet border.Flooding and mud slides hit the Rasuaw region in the morning on Wednesday, killing at least 162 people, police said.  Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said 826 people are missing, with the number of missing tourists said to be more than 529.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he is in touch with local authorities and "will do everything we can" to support British nationals, urging those in the region "to follow guidance from the local authorities and follow our travel advice". A 13-year-old is the youngest person from the UK still missing.The UK Foreign Office said it is working closely with Nepalese authorities "following concerning reports of British nationals who are missing" and has encouraged Brits to follow local guidance and "remain alert to the changing situation".According to police, 113 of the missing tourists are Nepalese, and 54 are from the US.According to the company's travel logs, shared with the Press Association, the age of the missing British citizens ranges from 13 to 65.Alpine Eco Trek said the youngest member of the group is believed to be a 13-year-old girl, according to PA.It also reported four of the firm's Nepali tour guides are also missing. The company's manager Kumar Adhikari said he was in contact with the guides until 08:40 when they were expected to be at Tibet's immigration office, but their phones were disconnected."We were hoping that inside it was safe," he told PA, "but later the video came from China's government which [showed] even Tibet's side was hit by the flood."Adhikari said he was "slowly responding to" the families of the Britons but has been unable to give them any updates, adding he has been in contact with the British consulate and forwarded them copies of the clients' passports."I feel so sad. We are just thinking about what to do next...We are in pain at the moment, deep pain."Another tour company impacted by the flash floods, Himalayan Glacier US, told the BBC they have lost contact with a group of 47 guests and staff who where making a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, which included two British citizens.Kailash Journeys also reported a group of 27 guests and staff missing, with a spokesperson saying they were last in contact with them early Wednesday morning local time.A list of names provided to the BBC included two men who are British citizens.Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said he is "deeply concerned" by news of the flash flooding, and wrote on social media: "All my thoughts are with those affected and with British nationals in the area and their relatives here at home".In a joint statement with Australia, the EU, Finland, France, Norway and Switzerland, the UK embassy in Nepal urged British nationals in Nepal to "exercise caution in affected areas".

title: Neath woman alleged to have mis-sold horses via Facebook
description: Facebook seller mis-sold me a horse that kicked my daughter in the headImage source, FacebookImage caption, Tasha Lee Hopkins, who is alleged to have
body: Facebook seller mis-sold me a horse that kicked my daughter in the headImage source, FacebookImage caption, Tasha Lee Hopkins, who is alleged to have mis-sold horses, regularly posts photos to Facebook of herself riding horsesByLily HewitsonBBC WalesUpdated 1 hour agoWhen her teenage daughter was lying motionless on the floor after being kicked in the head by a horse, Fiona feared the worst."For a moment, I thought she was dead," she said. "I thought she had broken her neck."The horse Fiona bought six weeks earlier via Facebook was marketed as a "teenager's dream" but during a riding lesson, it bucked and bolted with her daughter partially on it before kicking her in the head.Now Fiona, whose name has been changed to protect her daughter's identity, is one of five women who have told the BBC they were mis-sold horses that were either unsafe to ride or had life-limiting conditions by horse seller Tasha Lee Hopkins.Hopkins has been contacted for comment.Fiona's 13-year-old daughter was rushed to hospital in an ambulance with concussion and spent about two weeks recovering at home from her injuries after the incident at a riding arena in south Wales."You could see on the side of her helmet, the hoofmark where she got kicked in the head," said Fiona.  "I was thinking, 'oh my gosh she's going to be paralysed.' It was just awful."Fiona witnessed the "terrifying" moment and was "absolutely horrified" to later discover she had been sold a horse that had never been sufficiently trained to ride."I trusted Tasha. I believed what she said and she sold us a horse that wasn't fit for purpose, it wasn't fit for a child to be riding," added Fiona.Image source, FacebookImage caption, Photos posted online by Tasha Lee Hopkins suggest she has been involved with horses for many yearsA leading horse welfare organisation has warned of "too many cases" where horses that cannot be ridden are given away or sold "until they end up in a really poor situation".World Horse Welfare said unlike other animals such as dogs, there are no regulatory or voluntary industry standards for horse trading, so it is "vital" that sellers and prospective buyers do their due diligence.Fiona bought the 14-year-old horse from Hopkins in December 2024.It had been advertised on Facebook group CT Sports Horses, which is run by Hopkins and another person, and describes itself as selling "safe sports horses" that have six-month warranties."We went to view the horse and met Tasha and she seemed lovely, it all felt very genuine," said Fiona."It wasn't until the horse arrived back at home that it all started to unravel."After the incident, Fiona tracked down the horse's original owner. They said they had owned the animal since it was two - and during that time the horse had not been ridden.Fiona claims Hopkins didn't disclose this information when she bought the animal.The BBC has found this was not the first time Hopkins, from Neath near Swansea, is alleged to have mis-sold a horse in the last seven years.While five women have claimed they were mis-sold horses by Hopkins, another two have told us they had concerns about her operation.Image source, Kayleigh SweetImage caption, Kayleigh Sweet bought Otto after her previous horse was put down, but within weeks she discovered he had the same conditionOne buyer alleged she was sold a horse for riding by Hopkins that had an undisclosed broken back.Another claimed Hopkins sold a horse for showjumping which had such severe arthritis, a vet had previously recommended it should be put down.That horse, Otto was bought for £6,250 by Kayleigh Sweet in March last year after the 37-year-old saw an advert on Facebook and was told by Hopkins it had recently been checked and cleared by a vet."[Hopkins said] he was a 'perfectly sound five-year-old'," recalled Sweet.But within a week of owning him, Sweet noticed Otto - a warmblood breed that was about 17 hands tall - had gone lame and was struggling to walk.When she looked at his medical history, she noticed there was "no history, no vaccinations, nothing, and that's really unusual".She then tracked down Otto's original owner, who told her that as a three-year-old he had been diagnosed with chronic arthritis in his leg. Image source, FacebookImage caption, Otto was advertised on Facebook as a 'lovely event horse' but it later emerged he was lame, with chronic arthiritisSweet said she was told the horse had been operated on but it had not improved enough for riding - and the vet had advised them to put the animal down.Sweet said the then owner gifted him as a companion horse instead - meaning he would be kept as a pet. But Otto ended up being sold and ultimately owned by Hopkins.An examination by Sweet's own vet confirmed the diagnosis but when she told Hopkins, she said she refused to honour the six-month warranty.Otto's arthritis diagnosis was devastating for Sweet, who'd previously had to have another horse put down due to the exact same issue."I just had to relive it all over again and it's horrible," added Sweet, from the Vale of Glamorgan.She took legal action and earlier this month Hopkins appeared at the County Court in Swansea where she was ordered to pay Sweet £11,000 in damages and expenses, which had been due in October 2025.During the legal proceedings, Otto was returned to Hopkins. Sweet doesn't know what has happened to him since.Image caption, Tasha Lee Hopkins, seen in the striped top, was surrounded by people as she left court in Swansea last weekAnother person, Hayley Vaughan bought a horse called Bonnie for £1,400 from Hopkins for her 16-year-old daughter Amber after seeing an advert on Facebook in 2019.But the 55-year-old said her daughter only rode her once before they had to call the vet."She looked really uncomfortable, we decided to get her x-rayed," recalled Vaughan from Haverfordwest.Scans showed Bonnie had a serious back injury and a painful spinal condition."The vet said there was no way she could ever be ridden," added Vaughan.After the horse kicked out with both hind legs in the stable - a sign that it was in pain - she said the vet told her "don't you ever let your child ride that horse".Vaughan contacted Hopkins after the discovery."She [said she] would take the horse back but not give me my money back."Image source, Hayley VaughanImage caption, Hayley Vaughan bought a horse from Tasha Lee Hopkins for her daughter Amber, who was then 16, in 2019"There was no way I was giving that horse back to her. I wish I'd had the courage to take her to court."Vaughan found Bonnie a retirement home to ensure she could live out her life in the right conditions but says she lost all the money she'd spent on the horse.The BBC put all of these allegations to Hopkins but she did not respond to our questions. The BBC also asked Facebook's owner Meta about the CT Sports Horses Facebook group and associated adverts on the site - and it said it has now "removed the content brought to our attention for violating our policies".The five women who claim they were mis-sold horses by Hopkins told the BBC they viewed the animals but didn't have a pre-purchase examination by a vet.Image source, Hayley VaughanImage caption, Teenager Amber Vaughan only got to ride her new horse Bonnie once before discovering she was injured and should never be riddenWorld Horse Welfare recommends to all prospective buyers to view the horse in person, get it checked by your own vet and ride - if appropriate."Just be really vigilant, do your homework, go through the passport," added Sweet."You've got to do your research."She is now calling for horse passports to be made digital because some buyers have said the paper format can lead to key information about the horse's medical history being undisclosed during the sale."I don't think I'll ever find peace until there's some underpinning security for animals and for people when it comes to processes like this," said Sweet."People should have the truth from day dot and things aren't masked, because you can quite easily get a replacement passport for a horse that has nothing in it."The Welsh government said: "While paper passports remain a legal requirement, we recognise the opportunities digital technologies may offer to strengthen equine identification records."

title: Susan Sarandon leads tributes to Rocky Horror Picture Show co-star Tim Curry
description: But he was perhaps best known for his zany role as the cross-dressing Dr Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Picture Show. He first played the part on
body: But he was perhaps best known for his zany role as the cross-dressing Dr Frank-N-Furter in The Rocky Horror Picture Show. He first played the part on stage before the movie adaptation that propelled him to cult stardom.Sarandon, who played the heroine Janet Weiss in movie, praised Curry as "a funny, sexy, original"."Thank you Tim for meaning so much to so many people."Curry's longtime manager and friend Marcia Hurwitz confirmed he "passed away peacefully at his home in Toluca Lake, Los Angeles on August 25". Australian actress Nell Campbell, who starred alongside Curry in The Rocky Horror Picture Show, told the BBC: "I feel like the head of our family has just died because he was the head of the Rocky Horror family."Welsh actor Luke Evans, who played Frank-N-Furter in a Broadway revival, called Curry "a force, a bright fierce flame, an exquisite charm".In a letter he recently wrote to Curry, Evans thanked him for his fearlessness and for "creating something so enduring, and for inspiring generations of actors to be a little braver than they thought they could be".The official Rocky Horror Picture Show on Broadway account similarly thanked the late actor for "giving the world a little more freedom, a little more fearlessness, and through the tears in our eyes, the courage to BE IT" - a nod to Curry's delivery of the famous line from the musical: "Don't dream it, be it."In a statement to Entertainment Weekly, writer and composer Richard O'Brien, who co-wrote the musical and film, remembered the actor as "a wonderful man by nature who was also a wonderful performer". "He never sought attention and never put himself before the roles that he played," O'Brien said. "He was, in short, a good egg and class act."Curry also starred in the 1996 film Muppet Treasure Island alongside Miss Piggy and Kermit the Frog. He was one of the few humans "to have earned the title of honorary Muppet", the Muppets account posted on Tuesday."As a performer he was unparalleled – witty, charming, unnerving, and deeply funny. We will always consider it one of our greatest treasures to have been part of Long John Silver's crew," it added.American comedy icon Carol Burnett shared a clip of Curry's turn as her smarmy brother in Annie, posting on social media that "nobody could play lovable villains better than he could".Rob Schneider, who played the bellboy to Curry's uppity hotel clerk in Home Alone 2, also praised Curry as a "sensational character actor". "A truly gifted performer of stage and screen, his one eyebrow could say more than most actors entire bodies," Schneider said. "I am grateful to have the rare gift of watching him work, he made you better just standing near him."Clue co-star and Better Call Saul actor Michael McKean said on social media that his last conversation with Curry was about "life and love and laughter"."The grim physical state he found himself in has now ended, a blessing. Our blessing was that we had Tim Curry in our lives. RIP, my friend," he wrote.Two other stars of Clue, where Curry played a butler, Christopher Lloyd and Lesley Ann Warren, also paid tribute on social media.Lloyd shared a photo of Curry from the film along with a heart emoji and Warren called Curry a "dear companion in crime"."The brilliant, hilarious, hysterically funny, magician of artistry has left us," she said. "What an unbelievable joy to have shared a soundstage with him and to engage with such a master talent. I adored him. Bless his wild and inspired soul."

schema.headline: Susan Sarandon leads tributes to Rocky Horror Picture Show co-star Tim Curry
